description: Tests the question: if AI improves itself and becomes more efficient, will human demand still be large enough to keep the data centres busy - or will they be dismantled like the US railroad network? Three reference cases are encoded: the US rail network (peak 1916, ~45% of route miles removed while freight output grew), the 1990s fibre glut (only a small share of laid fibre was lit in 2002, yet the asset later carried the cloud), and the current AI build-out. The key modelled distinction is asset lifetime: long-lived shells, power hookups and land versus short-lived accelerators. Measured values carry a source; projections and structural estimates carry 'assumed value' with a numeric confidence (0-1) so weak assumptions surface first. All content in English per project convention. Patched to 0.0.2 with the competing scaffolding hypothesis: today's high token count per task is largely error-correction and missing memory rather than irreducible work, so per-task compute at fixed difficulty should fall as models and harnesses improve. The decisive quantity is therefore the ratio between the yearly fall in compute per task at fixed difficulty and the yearly rise in the difficulty of tasks delegated.

words.name: artificial intelligence

words.name: demand

words.name: capacity
words.description: the maximum output an installed facility can sustain.

words.name: efficiency

words.name: utilization
words.description: the share of installed capacity actually in productive use.

words.name: data centre

words.name: token

words.name: price

words.name: programming

words.name: agentic
words.description: of a workload in which the model itself issues further calls in loops and tool chains, so that one human request generates many model requests.

words.name: verification
words.description: the process of establishing that a claim or output is true; here the human- or system-side capacity to check AI output before acting on it.

words.name: Jevons

words.name: paradox

words.name: freight

words.name: fibre

words.name: lifetime

words.name: capital expenditure

words.name: power

words.name: minimum
words.description: the least amount considered plausible.

words.name: likely
words.description: the outcome carrying the highest probability mass under the assumed scenario.

words.name: maximum
words.description: the greatest amount considered plausible.

words.name: measured
words.description: ascertained by an external source rather than assumed; provenance qualifier.

words.name: assumed
words.description: estimated or projected rather than sourced; provenance qualifier carrying a confidence.

words.name: value
words.description: a stored number in the graph; combined with 'measured' or 'assumed' to mark provenance.

words.name: confidence
words.description: degree of belief, 0 to 1, that an assumed value is correct; low confidence marks an assumption worth checking first.

words.name: task
words.description: a unit of delegated work with a defined completion criterion; the natural denominator for agent compute cost.

words.name: difficulty
words.description: how demanding a task is, held separate from how efficiently a given system solves it.

words.name: orchestration
words.description: the harness layer that mediates control flow, loop budgets, retry policy and tool input/output around a model.

words.name: overhead
words.description: resource consumption that does not contribute to the result, here tokens spent on retries, replayed context and redundant reasoning.

words.name: saving
words.description: the reduction in resource consumption achieved by a change, expressed as a share of the prior level.

words.name: repetition
words.description: the property of a task recurring in near-identical form, which makes its solution path cacheable.

words.name: ingest
words.description: the reading of external state, such as a codebase or document corpus, that a system must perform regardless of its own capability.

triples.name: measured value
triples.description: provenance qualifier: the number comes from an external reference.

triples.name: assumed value
triples.description: provenance qualifier: the number is an estimate carrying a confidence.

triples.name: railroad network
triples.description: the US freight rail network, measured in route miles of line owned or operated.

triples.name: route mile
triples.description: one mile of line, counted once regardless of how many parallel tracks it carries.

triples.name: network peak
triples.description: the highest extent a network reached before contraction; for US rail this was 1916, decades before its traffic peak.

triples.name: network reduction
triples.description: the share of the peak network subsequently abandoned; the quantity the railroad analogy turns on.

triples.name: freight share
triples.description: the share of national long-distance ton-miles still carried by the reduced rail network - the evidence that contraction was concentration, not demand collapse.

triples.name: lit fibre
triples.description: the share of laid optical fibre actually carrying traffic; the 1990s glut's utilization measure.

triples.name: token volume
triples.description: tokens processed per month, the throughput measure of inference demand.

triples.name: inference price
triples.description: the price of a unit of inference at fixed capability; falling fast, which is the efficiency term in the question.

triples.name: programming share
triples.description: the share of tokens generated by coding and agent workflows rather than by direct human questions.

triples.name: agentic demand
triples.description: demand in which the model's own loops, not the number of human questions, set the token volume; the reason 'enough questions' is the wrong demand unit.

triples.name: verification limit
triples.description: thesis: once compute is near-free, the binding constraint on useful AI demand is the capacity to check outputs, not the supply of questions or of compute.

triples.name: Jevons paradox
triples.description: efficiency gains lowering unit cost raise rather than lower total consumption, as long as demand is sufficiently elastic.

triples.name: data centre capacity
triples.description: installed data centre capacity, measured as connected electrical load.

triples.name: data centre utilization
triples.description: the share of installed data centre capacity in productive use; the quantity the question asks about.

triples.name: accelerator lifetime
triples.description: the economic life of AI accelerators; short, which is what breaks the railroad and fibre analogies.

triples.name: shell lifetime
triples.description: the economic life of buildings, cooling and grid connections; long, like rail and fibre.

triples.name: accelerator capex share
triples.description: the share of data centre capital expenditure sunk into short-lived silicon rather than long-lived shell.

triples.name: gigawatt power
triples.description: electrical load measured in gigawatts.

triples.name: megawatt power
triples.description: electrical load measured in megawatts.

triples.name: trillion token
triples.description: token counts measured in trillions.

triples.name: yearly factor
triples.description: a multiplicative rate of change per year.

triples.name: AI capacity
triples.description: the share of data centre capacity dedicated to AI training and inference.

triples.name: compute per task
triples.description: compute consumed to complete one task; falls with model and harness quality at fixed difficulty.

triples.name: task difficulty
triples.description: the demandingness of the tasks actually delegated; rises as per-task cost falls, which is the counter-term to the scaffolding hypothesis.

triples.name: orchestration overhead
triples.description: the share of tokens attributable to harness design rather than to the work itself; the quantity the scaffolding hypothesis says will shrink toward zero.

triples.name: orchestration saving
triples.description: measured cost reduction from swapping only the orchestration layer, with tasks and models held constant.

triples.name: model choice saving
triples.description: cost reduction available from model choice alone on the same workload; the comparison baseline showing harness beats model as a cost lever.

triples.name: repetition share
triples.description: the share of workload that recurs in cacheable form, and is therefore the part most exposed to near-total token elimination.

triples.name: ingest share
triples.description: the share of tokens spent reading external state, which does not shrink with model capability and forms the floor under per-task compute.

sources.name: AAR short history freight railroads
sources.description: Association of American Railroads, A Short History of U.S. Freight Railroads: by 1917 about 1,500 US railroads operated around 254,000 miles; mileage had already peaked in 1916 and employment peaked in 1920.

sources.name: FRA freight rail overview
sources.description: US Federal Railroad Administration: the US freight rail network runs on almost 140,000 route miles; rail carries roughly 28 percent of US freight movement measured in ton-miles.

sources.name: Fabricated Knowledge telecom bubble
sources.description: Fabricated Knowledge, Lessons from History: The Rise and Fall of the Telecom Bubble, citing the Wall Street Journal that only 2.7 percent of laid fibre was in use in 2002 after the overbuild.

sources.name: SGNL Jevons inference 2026
sources.description: SGNL Intelligence, 28 Mar 2026, on the OpenRouter State of AI study (over 100 trillion tokens analysed): programming rose from roughly 11 percent of token volume in early 2025 to over 50 percent by March 2026; agent-driven workflow tokens exceed half of platform output.

sources.name: arXiv inference economics 2026
sources.description: arXiv 2607.07207, Memory Scarcity, Open Models, and the Restructuring of the AI Industry 2026-2030: Google token volume from about 9.7 trillion per month in May 2024 to 480 trillion at I/O 2025, 1.3 quadrillion by October 2025 and 3.2 quadrillion by May 2026, a stated 7x year-over-year rate.

sources.name: SSRN Jevons AI infrastructure 2026
sources.description: Do, Tuan Anh, The Jevons Paradox in AI Infrastructure: Efficiency, Rebound, and the Limits of Cost Reduction, 15 June 2026, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6775299; companion work reports inference prices falling roughly 40x per year at fixed capability while token volumes grew about sevenfold year over year.

sources.name: Gartner JLL data centre 2026
sources.description: Market summary of Gartner and JLL figures: global data centre power about 132 GW in 2026, up roughly 27 percent; about 25 GW absorbed in North America in the first half of 2026, twice the prior-year period; the five largest hyperscalers announced roughly 710 billion US dollars of 2026 investment.

sources.name: Bitkom data centres Germany 2025
sources.description: Bitkom, November 2025: German data centre connected load grew 9 percent in 2025 to 2,980 MW and should pass 5,000 MW by 2030; AI-specific capacity is 530 MW, forecast to quadruple to 2,020 MW by 2030; power use reached 21.3 billion kWh in 2025.

sources.name: KKR AI infrastructure 2026
sources.description: KKR, Beyond the Bubble, May 2026: fast accelerator refresh cycles mean temporary overbuilds behave like rolling upgrades rather than stranded assets, and power - grid queues, transformer lead times, permitting - rather than capital is the binding limit on overbuild.

sources.name: IEEE ComSoc AI capex versus fibre
sources.description: IEEE ComSoc Technology Blog comparing AI capex to the 1990s fibre build-out: hyperscalers generate far more cash than the 1990s fibre builders, but big tech issued about 100 billion US dollars of bonds in 2026 to fund AI capex, with record credit-default-swap protection demanded against it.

sources.name: arXiv harness effect 2026
sources.description: arXiv 2607.06906, The Harness Effect, July 2026: 22 locked enterprise tasks on six models under two orchestration layers with everything else held constant; blended cost per task falls 41 percent, up to 61 percent on one model, while moving from the most to the least expensive model saves only 36 percent; names the prevailing pattern token maxing, buying capability with tokens so that tokens per task grow faster than task value.

sources.name: Glean token efficiency 2026
sources.description: Glean, June 2026, summarising a 2026 Stevens Institute analysis and the LOOP Skill Engine paper: unconstrained agents spent 5 to 8 US dollars per task and dynamic turn limits cut that by 24 percent at comparable quality; prompt caching cuts input token cost by up to 90 percent; compiling successful traces into branch-free recipes achieved 93.3 percent token savings on daily repeated tasks and 99.98 percent on high-frequency operations.

sources.name: arXiv token economics agents 2026
sources.description: arXiv 2605.09104, Token Economics for LLM Agents: formalises the harness layer as an economic design surface and finds that harness-level choices such as loop budgets, retry policies and observation truncation often dominate model-level differences in end-to-end token cost.
